title: IS INTERIOR WOOD USE PSYCHOLOGICALLY BENEFICIAL? A REVIEW OF PSYCHOLOGICAL RESPONSES TOWARD WOOD
authors: Anders Q. Nyrud and Tina Bringslimark, 2010
review_question: To investigate whether interior wood use might be psychologically beneficial by reviewing studies that have investigated psychological responses toward wood.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Studies published in peer-reviewed English journals (with one proceeding included); focused on interior wood use (excluding outdoor wood/forests); excluded studies on computerized pictures of wood; excluded studies related to indoor environmental quality (thermal, acoustic, air quality) as these are physical outcomes, not psychological benefits.

findings.antecedent: Interior spaces with large proportions of wood
findings.consequent: Perception of the space as 'warm' and 'natural'
findings.source: Visual Perception of Wood, Summing up
findings.quote: Interior spaces containing large proportions of wood are often described as “warm” and "natural"

findings.antecedent: Number of knots in wood panels
findings.quote: there was a clear linear relationship between the number of knots in the wooden wall panels and the subjective noticeability

findings.antecedent: Number and amount of knots in wood surfaces
findings.quote: multiple knots had a negative impact on people's preferences.

findings.source: Tactile Sensation of Wood, Summing up
findings.quote: tactile contact with wood did not induce higher levels of stress responses

findings.consequent: Positive attitudes and preference over other materials
findings.quote: In general, people have positive attitudes toward wood and interior wood use. Wood is also most often preferred over other materials

findings.antecedent: Wood species name vs. actual wood appearance
findings.quote: there exists a discrepancy between consumers' opinions on wood species when they are based on the species name compared with the wood appearance.

findings.antecedent: Visual properties of wood (homogeneity, moderate complexity, naturalness)
findings.quote: people prefer settings or elements that have a moderate degree of complexity... harmonious or homogenous visual surfaces are important attributes for preferences

findings.antecedent: Presence of wood in indoor settings (e.g., living rooms, offices)
findings.consequent: Preference for relaxation, perceived suitability for living, preference as employment place
findings.source: Wood in different settings, Summing up
findings.quote: organizations with significantly visible wood products in their office environments were preferred as places of potential employment... great preference for relaxation was obtained from the photographs showing wood materials

findings.antecedent: Visual exposure to wood in actual-sized living rooms (different wood ratios)
findings.consequent: Psychophysiological responses (pulse rate, blood pressure) and mood/subjective evaluation
findings.source: Psychophysiological Responses Toward Wood, Summing up
findings.quote: pulse rate decreased in the ordinary room, whereas contradictory to expectations, the pulse rate increased in the room in which wood was added... diastolic blood pressure decreased significantly in all three rooms.

findings.antecedent: Visual stimulation by hinoki wall panel
findings.source: Psychophysiological Responses Toward Wood, Summing up
findings.quote: feelings of depression/dejection were significantly lower for the visual stimulation by the hinoki wall panel than the control.

synthesis_conclusions: People generally have positive attitudes toward wood and interior wood use, perceiving it as natural, warm, and healthy.
Wood is often preferred over other materials, and certain wood properties (e.g., homogeneity, moderate complexity, naturalness, fewer knots) are consistently preferred.

There is some evidence that responses toward wood are measurable by psychophysiological outcomes, indicating potential psychological beneficial effects, though findings are often mixed or inconsistent.
The natural characteristics of wood are important factors influencing preferences.
The inclusion of wood in indoor settings can increase preference for relaxation and perceived suitability of a space.
evidence_gaps: Lack of research on which specific psychological processes are engaged in generating psychological benefits from nature in indoor settings.
Absence of theory development as a main purpose in previous research within this field.
Insufficient knowledge to translate research findings into guidelines for designing nearby nature.
Limited understanding of spatial conditions needed to promote beneficial effects from natural elements indoors.
Uncertainty regarding the strength of relationships between nature in different indoor settings and beneficial effects.
Need for more studies to distinguish individual, cultural, and evolutionary contributions to wood preferences.
Need to investigate how uniquely natural forms generate psychological benefits by modulating perceived stimulation levels.
limitations: Lack of homogeneity in research design, experimental manipulations, and outcome measures across reviewed studies, preventing meta-analysis.
Review limited to peer-reviewed English-language journals, excluding studies in other languages (e.g., French, Japanese).
Studies often did not induce stress before measuring stress recovery, making interpretation of physiological responses difficult.
Potential for extraneous factors in experimental situations to influence responses.
Difficulty in interpreting physiological measures when subjective evaluations of rooms are not significantly different.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: The innate human tendency to connect with nature extends to natural materials like wood, contributing to positive psychological responses.
Exposure to natural elements, including wood, can facilitate the restoration of directed attention and reduce mental fatigue.
Interacting with natural environments or materials like wood can lead to physiological and psychological stress reduction.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper reviews a multi-step causal mechanism connecting the presence of wood in interior spaces to various psychological benefits, often starting with sensory perception and cognitive appraisal.

steps.from_construct: Presence of wood in interior spaces
steps.to_construct: Sensory perception of wood (visual, tactile, olfactory cues)
Cognitive appraisal (e.g., perceived naturalness, warmth, comfort, authenticity)
Affective responses (e.g., feelings of relaxation, comfort, positive mood)
Physiological responses (e.g., reduced heart rate, lower blood pressure, decreased cortisol levels)
Psychological benefits (e.g., stress reduction, improved well-being, enhanced cognitive performance)
